newsitem.title: UK: Br Gas sees interconnector capital hiatus.
newsitem.headline: Br Gas sees interconnector capital hiatus.

text.p: British Gas Plc chairman Richard Giordano said on Wednesday that the company faced a "hiatus" over finance for the interconnector project designed to link the gas pipelines of Britain and continental Europe.
He blamed the problem on stringent price proposals by gas industry regulator Clare Spottiswoode, which British Gas has appealed against to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
Giordano said the proposals had caused British Gas's cost of capital to rise so sharply that its shareholders "will not allow us to make discretionary investments".
Speaking to parliament's Trade and Industry Committee, Giordano said the referral to the MMC would stall decisions of importance to the gas industry as a whole.
"We for example have got an investment programme planned in Transco, the utility. Some of that investment is discretionary," Giordano told the committee.
"Some of it for example relates to the Interconnector. We are clearly building an interconnector from Bacton (eastern England) to Zeebrugge (Belgium)."
"The cost of capital that is now on the table... is inadequate. Our shareholders will not allow us to make discretiionary investments as that cost of capital."
"There is a kind of hiatus here in which we have to sort through what do we do while we are waiting for a decision on cost of capital."

Spottiswoode has proposed that TransCo, the part of British Gas responsible for a pipe network, should cut charges to gas suppliers by 20 pct in 1997 and then by 6.5 pct below inflation for the following four years.
British Gas has a 40 percent share in the 500 million stg Interconnector project on which work started this month.

Other companies involved are British Petroleum Plc with 10 percent, Elf Aquitaine SA with 10 percent, Gazprom with 10 percent, Distrigaz with five percent, Ruhrgas with five percent, Amerada Hess with five percent and National Power with five percent.
Giordano said the industry's regulatory system was too dependent on a single figure -- at present Spottiswoode -- and should be reformed by creating a regulatory board with non-executive directors.
"We need to get out from under the single authority of the one regulator with vast powers," he said.
